ConditionalQA scores an answer with conditions by using a scoring function that combines the accuracy of the predicted answer and the accuracy of the predicted conditions. Conditions are restricted to be HTML elements in the document, and the F1 score equals 1 only if all required conditions are correctly selected. If no condition is required, the model should predict an empty set. This evaluation approach treats condition selection as a retrieval task, emphasizing precise identification of all necessary conditions for the answer to hold true [T2][T10].

The questions in ConditionalQA are hard because they require understanding complex internal logic within long documents, including conjunctions, disjunctions, exceptions, and multi-hop reasoning. The questions are asked without knowing the answers, making them naturally incomplete and requiring models to find all possible answers along with their applicable conditions. The documents have complex structures unlike typical Wikipedia pages, and answering requires compositional logical reasoning across multiple parts of the text. Additionally, the dataset includes various question types (yes/no, extractive, multiple answers, not answerable), and models must jointly predict answers and their conditions, which is challenging. Existing state-of-the-art models perform poorly, especially in selecting conditions, with accuracy dropping significantly when conditions are jointly evaluated with answers [T1][T3][T5][T8][T9].

Baseline methods like ETC and DocHopper are adapted to predict answers and conditions, but they are limited to predicting one answer and use binary classification for condition selection. The difficulty in condition selection is a major source of errors [T7][T11][T8].

The scoring function computes embeddings for each document independently and combines them via a neural network (MLP) to produce the score [T1][T4][E12][E15][E18].

KG-FiD incorporates knowledge-graph structure into a text model by constructing a passage graph where vertices represent text passages and edges represent relationships derived from an external knowledge graph (English Wikidata). It employs a two-stage passage reranking process using graph neural networks (GNNs), specifically Graph Attention Networks (GAT), to model structural and semantic information of passages. In the first stage, passage embeddings from a dense passage retriever (DPR) initialize GNN node representations to rerank a large set of candidate passages. The second stage uses embeddings from intermediate layers of the reader encoder to rerank a smaller candidate set more accurately. Only top reranked passages are fed into the Fusion-in-Decoder (FiD) reader for answer generation. This approach leverages the knowledge graph to establish structural relationships among retrieved passages, improving passage selection and reducing computation cost while maintaining or improving QA performance [T1][T6][T7][T9][T10][E3][E4][E5][E7][E11][E12][C1].

ReasoningLM integrates knowledge-graph structure directly into a pre-trained language model (PLM) by introducing a subgraph-aware self-attention mechanism that imitates graph neural networks to perform structured reasoning over KG subgraphs. This mechanism attends to neighboring nodes and relations in the KG, enabling fine-grained interaction and knowledge sharing between the question and the KG subgraph within the PLM architecture. ReasoningLM also uses an adaptation tuning strategy with synthesized subgraphs and questions to adapt the PLM parameters to this new input format and attention mechanism. This unified approach simplifies the typical two-module architecture (PLM + GNN) by embedding structural reasoning capabilities directly into the PLM, enhancing both question understanding and KG reasoning [T2][T4][T5][E1][E6][E7][C2].

In summary, KG-FiD brings KG structure into a text model by building and leveraging a passage graph with GNN-based reranking stages feeding into a FiD reader, while ReasoningLM embeds KG structural reasoning directly into the PLM via a subgraph-aware self-attention mechanism and adaptation tuning.

Specifically, the scoring function sem+c(·) multiplies the semantic similarity score of the predicted answer to the gold answer sem(·) by the F1 score of the predicted conditions against the gold conditions at the HTML element level. The questions in ConditionalQA are hard because they require understanding complex internal logic within long documents, including conjunctions, disjunctions, exceptions, and multi-hop reasoning. The documents have complex structure and logical relationships that are crucial for answering questions. Questions are asked without knowing the answers, making them naturally incomplete and requiring models to find all possible answers along with their applicable conditions. This demands compositional logical reasoning across complex contexts. Additionally, questions can be yes/no, extractive, multi-answer, or not answerable, increasing difficulty. Existing models perform poorly, especially in selecting conditions, with accuracy dropping significantly when answers and conditions are jointly evaluated [T1][T3][T5][T8][T9].

In summary, ConditionalQA evaluates answers with conditions by a combined answer and condition accuracy metric at the HTML element level, and its questions are challenging due to complex document logic, multi-hop reasoning, incomplete questions, and diverse answer types requiring extensive reasoning [T2][T10][T1][T3][T5].

The model "translates" a query sequence (head entity and relation) into a path sequence by encoding the query and previously generated path tokens and decoding the next token autoregressively. The Transformer encoder-decoder architecture allows SQUIRE to generate paths in an end-to-end fashion, enabling it to dynamically complete missing edges along the path [T1][T3][E2]. During inference, beam search is used to generate the reasoning path of maximum length \( N \) from the query [T4][E3].

In summary, SQUIRE samples paths up to length 3 for training and employs a Transformer encoder-decoder model to convert a query into a path sequence [T3][T1].

This mechanism is integrated into a constrained masking framework to jointly model attention over the question, KG to question, and KG itself, allowing fine-grained interaction and knowledge sharing between the question and KG subgraph. ReasoningLM adapts the PLM parameters through tuning on synthesized subgraphs and questions, enabling unified question understanding and structured KG reasoning without separate GNN modules [T2][T3][T4][T5][E1][E6][E7].

In summary, KG-FiD brings KG structure into text models by using GNNs over passage graphs for reranking within FiD, while ReasoningLM embeds KG structural reasoning directly into the PLM via a subgraph-aware self-attention mechanism that mimics GNNs, enabling unified reasoning and question understanding.
